metaDescription: Enter Sovereign Call: Origins — An Epoch, by Michael Vaylin Keyes. A novel of contested legacy, divided loyalties, and the cost of conviction. Read an opening excerpt and discover the author.
eyebrow: A novel by Michael Vaylin Keyes
tagline: In the shadow of a vanished king, even loyalty has a price.
footnote: A legacy contested. A conviction tested.
storyDeck: A story of faith, power, and the fault line between obedience and conviction.
story: A vanished king. A legacy claimed by opposing powers. Civilizations that have built their identities around what they believe he stood for.
For the Dominion and the Reformation, the past is more than history. It is a justification. And in the space between loyalty and conviction, people must live with the cost.

In Ianis, a city held in endless evening, High Centurion Tarrik Walcur returns from the front to a summons at Crownwatch. His soldiers are still at war. The Empire has a ceremony waiting for him. He knows the difference between serving a cause and becoming its symbol.
Sovereign Call: Origins asks what remains of faithfulness when the institutions that demand our obedience begin to lose sight of the truth they were built to protect.
excerptIntro: Enter the city of endless evening.
An opening passage from Sovereign Call: Origins.
excerpt: Amber clouds drift across the evening sky, veiling the silhouette of Ianis. Gulls wheel through the humid air, their cries lost beneath market bells, engines, and the distant labor of furnaces. The dying sun catches the city’s bronze towers before slipping below the horizon.
It will rise tomorrow in the same place. Here, evening never ends.

Ianis encircles its central mountain in a vast gyrosphere, its layered districts turning slowly around the ancient peak. Transit bridges span the rings like strands of a metallic web. Power conduits descend from the upper city into the depths of the world, feeding a metropolis trillions have called home. Crimson banners hang from towers, streets, and elevated railways, each bearing the bronze insignia of a central spike guarded by the halves of a broken shield.
Glory through power. Order through submission.
At the heart of the turning city, Crownwatch broods above it all.

The fortress crowns the mountain, separated from the people it governs by height, stone, and history. Its oldest foundations were laid during the reign of the Good King, when the mountain served as a refuge rather than a throne. Everything above them belongs to the centuries that followed. Carbon columns climb from the rock into halls of gold and bronze, built with the proportions of giants. Towers pierce the amber clouds. Their highest battlements disappear into light.

A single Telemy gunship descends toward the fortress through the haze. Its engines burn unevenly, bruising the atmosphere with black vapor. Sea-blue embers smolder across the scored plating of its left flank, remnants of its last encounter with the Reformation. Inside the commons module, the lights flicker with every correction of the damaged engine.
“High Centurion, we are beginning our final approach to Crownwatch.”
The pilot vanishes from the intercom, leaving the vibration of the gunship and the distant complaint of strained metal.
Tarrik Walcur releases his restraint. “Glory.”

He rises from the hard bench and secures his Cinderline rifle across his back. The weapon settles between his shoulder plates with a familiar weight. His cracked helm waits on the seat beside him, a blue-white fracture running across its visor. A Reformation bolt had put it there less than two days ago. He can still hear the soldier shouting before the shot struck.
Tarrik leaves the helm where it is.

Across the cabin, Lyessa Caedryn turns a radiant dagger between her gloved fingers. The blade catches the failing amber light in brief flashes. Her black hair is drawn into a single braid, and fresh scoring mars the crimson-bronze armor across her ribs.
“Try not to look so eager,” she says.
“We have survived most of our voyages together.”
“Most.” A faint smile touches her mouth. “A comforting record.”
The gunship shudders. Lyessa closes the dagger and crosses the cabin, her humor fading as she places a hand on his shoulder plate.
“This summons is unprecedented.”
“I know.”
“Whatever happens inside Crownwatch, we will leave differently than we entered.”
Beyond the rear viewport, Ianis fills the glass, all bronze towers and furnace light beneath the clouds.
“My soldiers are still on Proper,” he says. “Men who held the line because I told them it would matter. Some of them are lying in Reformation plasma, and I am here to receive a wreath.”
“You did not order the ceremony.”
“I accepted it.”
“You were summoned. Coming when summoned is generally part of being a soldier.”

He faces her. Wisps of auburn hair cling to his forehead, damp from the heat trapped inside his helm. “I do not want to become a poster for the Empire. My place is with them. With you. Out there. Not beneath some gilded statue while politicians recite the names of battles they never saw.”

Lyessa’s thumb rests against the Dominion sigil at the center of his breastplate. “Then let them have the ceremony. Let them place the wreath and tell themselves they made you.” Her gray-green eyes hold his. “You know better.”
The Telemy strikes the landing platform. The impact throws them both half a step sideways before the supports lock with a metallic groan.
“This is your stop, sir,” the pilot announces.
The rear ramp lowers. Warm air floods the cabin, carrying wet stone, incense, engine smoke, and food.
Tarrik and Lyessa share a final glance. Then he descends toward the identity waiting for him.
endLine: The rest of the story awaits.
bio: Michael Vaylin Keyes writes at the intersection of faith, art, and technology. With a background spanning storytelling, technology, and leadership, he builds worlds that are mythic in scale and deeply human at their heart.
He brings that perspective to Sovereign Call: Origins — a story concerned with the weight of loyalty, the responsibilities of power, and the courage it takes to follow conviction.
authorQuote: Rooted in the questions explored in the foreword, this is a story about the distance between preserving an institution and remaining faithful to its purpose — and about what following the King might cost.
